title: Helping a friend learn: a clue, not the answer
keyIdea: When a friend is stuck, the best help leaves the thinking to them. First let them try, and wait while they are still working. If they are stuck, give the smallest help that could work: ask 'What could you try?', then give a clue, then show a different example, then do it together. Give more help only if they are still stuck, and less as soon as they can do it. Telling the answer or doing it for them does not help, because then they cannot do the next one on their own. Kind words that praise the trying help a friend keep going.
familyTip: Next time your child helps a younger brother, sister or friend with a puzzle, count to five together before anyone helps. Then ask your child, 'What is the smallest clue you could give?' Afterwards, ask the friend to do one more on their own, and notice together whether they can.

visual.caption: Does it help your friend think, or does it do the thinking for them? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Which piece has a straight edge?
What sound does it start with?
Give it here, I will finish it.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort clues from answers, climb the help ladder, see who can do the next one, read if a friend is stuck, choose kind words.

kid: Your friend is stuck. You want to help. The best help lets your friend do the thinking. Then they learn how, and they can do the next one too.
First, wait. If your friend is still trying, let them think. If they stop and say they are stuck, give a small clue, like 'What could you try?' or 'Look at the straight edges.'
Still stuck? Give a bit more help. Show them a different one, then let them try. When they get it, stop helping and say well done.
Do not just tell the answer or do it for them. Then they have not learned how. Be kind: 'Good try! Look at this bit again.'
adult: Ages 6 to 7. This is the helper's side of learning together. In class it shows up as talk partners, peer tutoring and group work. The EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit rates peer tutoring as one of the better-evidenced approaches, about five months of extra progress on average, and stresses that tutors should be shown how to give hints and praise. Key words: clue (hint), help, stuck, try, explain, smallest help first.

Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976) called this scaffolding: the helper takes over only the parts the learner cannot yet do. Wood and Middleton (1975) found that mothers helped best when they were contingent. After a fail they gave a bit more help; after a success they gave less. That is the rule in the lab's help ladder: ask, then clue, then show a different example, then do it together, and step back as soon as the friend can do it.

Being handed the answer does not help much. In Webb's (1989) review of group work, children who got only answers, with no explanation, learned less, while those who gave explanations learned more. So helping well is good for both children. Waiting matters too: jumping in while a child is still working takes away the thinking that does the learning.

Common mistakes: telling the answer or doing it for them; starting with the biggest help; helping while a friend is still trying; carrying on helping after they have got it; and unkind words such as 'That is easy'. In the lab your child sorts 6 things helpers say, climbs the help ladder for 2 friends, says who can do the next one in 3 stories, decides wait, clue or well done for 5 friends, and sorts 5 helper phrases.

practice.prompt: Your friend is stuck on 9 + 4. What is the best first help?
choices: Take the pencil and write it
practice.hint: The best help leaves the thinking to your friend.
practice.explain: Asking 'What could you try?' is the smallest help. Your friend still does the thinking, so they learn how.

practice.prompt: Your friend is still counting on their fingers. What should you do?
practice.hint: Are they stuck, or still working?
practice.explain: They are still working it out, so wait. Helping now would take their thinking away.

practice.prompt: Your friend has put {a} of the 10 jigsaw pieces in. You give a clue and they find 1 more. How many pieces are in now?
practice.explain: {a} and 1 more make {=a+1} pieces. Your friend found the piece, so they learned where it goes.

practice.prompt: Your friend tried {a} times on their own before asking for help. With your clue, they tried {b} more times and got it. How many tries in all?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more tries.
practice.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b} tries. All that trying was your friend's own thinking, and that is how they learn.

practice.prompt: You gave a small clue and your friend got it right. What now?
choices: Say well done and stop helping
Do the next one for them
practice.hint: Ask yourself: does my friend still need help, now that they got it right?
practice.explain: They can do it now, so step back and say well done. Less help lets them do the next one alone.

pool.prompt: Which one is a clue, not the answer?
pool.hint: A clue helps your friend think for themselves.
pool.explain: 'Look at the first sound' is a clue. Your friend still reads the word, so they learn how.

pool.prompt: Ava was told the answer. Ben got a clue and worked it out. Who can do the next one alone?
pool.hint: Think about who did the thinking: hearing an answer, or working it out?
pool.explain: Ben worked it out himself, so he knows how. Ava only heard the answer, so she has not learned how yet.

pool.prompt: You asked 'What could you try?' and your friend is still stuck. What now?
pool.hint: Go up the help ladder one step.
pool.explain: Still stuck means a bit more help: one step up the ladder, a clue. Not the answer, and not walking away.

choices: Good try! Look at this bit again.
pool.explain: 'Good try! Look at this bit again' praises the trying and gives a clue. The others make a friend want to give up.

pool.prompt: You count to {a} before you help, so your friend has time to think. Then you count {b} more. How far did you count?
pool.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b}. Waiting gives your friend time to work it out.

pool.prompt: Your friend is stuck. Which is the smallest help?
pool.hint: Start at the bottom of the help ladder.
pool.explain: Asking 'What could you try?' is the smallest help. Doing it together is the biggest, for when nothing else worked.

pool.prompt: Why is doing it for your friend not much help?
choices: They cannot do the next one
pool.explain: If you do it, your friend does not learn how. Next time they will be stuck again.

pool.prompt: You help {a} friends. Each one needs 2 clues. How many clues do you give?
pool.hint: Count in 2s, once for each friend.
pool.explain: {a} friends with 2 clues each make {=a*2} clues. Each friend still did the thinking.

pool.prompt: Your friend says, 'I am stuck,' and has stopped. What do you do?
pool.hint: They have stopped, so they need some help, but not the answer.
pool.explain: They have stopped and asked, so give a small clue. Waiting longer leaves them stuck; the answer does the thinking for them.
